clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SPINK5, which encodes the serine protease inhibitor LEKTI
Classic triad of congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, a specific hair shaft defect (trichorrhexis invaginata, or 'bamboo hair'), and atopic diathesis with very high IgE
The characteristic migratory rash, ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, shows serpiginous double-edged scaling plaques
Neonates present with generalised erythroderma and scaling and are at high risk of dehydration, hypernatraemia, infection, and failure to thrive
Hair microscopy of the eyebrows may reveal the invaginated node defect more reliably than scalp hair
Skin barrier is markedly impaired, so percutaneous absorption of topical agents (including calcineurin inhibitors) can cause systemic toxicity
Confirmation is by SPINK5 genetic testing supported by absent LEKTI staining on immunohistochemistry
reference.pathophysiology: Netherton syndrome results from loss of function of the LEKTI protein, a multidomain serine protease inhibitor expressed in the granular and uppermost spinous layers of the epidermis. Without LEKTI, kallikrein-related peptidases (notably KLK5 and KLK7) are unrestrained, leading to premature and excessive degradation of corneodesmosomes and detachment of the stratum corneum. The result is a profoundly defective epidermal barrier with abnormal desquamation. Unchecked protease activity also drives proinflammatory and pro-allergic signalling, producing the severe atopic phenotype, elevated IgE, and susceptibility to cutaneous infection.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma / other autosomal recessive congenital ichthyoses
Immunodysregulation such as Omenn syndrome or other severe combined immunodeficiency presenting with erythroderma
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in the neonate
additionalInvestigations: Light microscopy of hair shafts (eyebrow and scalp) for trichorrhexis invaginata
Skin biopsy with immunostaining for LEKTI expression
Serum electrolytes and hydration status in neonates
Microbiological cultures when infection is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal hypernatraemic dehydration and thermoregulatory instability from barrier failure
Sepsis or recurrent severe skin and systemic infections
Failure to thrive and growth faltering
Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed topical agents (particularly calcineurin inhibitors)
reference.prognosis: It is a lifelong condition; the neonatal period carries the highest mortality risk from dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection, after which the phenotype tends to stabilise into ichthyosis linearis circumflexa with persistent atopy, though quality of life and growth remain affected.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as recalcitrant atopic dermatitis and delaying genetic evaluation
Applying topical calcineurin inhibitors over large areas of impaired barrier, risking systemic absorption and toxicity
Sampling only scalp hair and missing the diagnostic shaft defect best seen in eyebrows
Underestimating fluid, electrolyte, and infection risk in the erythrodermic neonate
management: Neonatal stabilisation is the priority, with careful fluid and electrolyte management, temperature regulation and nutritional support to counter transepidermal water loss, dehydration and hypernatraemia
Restore the skin barrier with liberal bland emollients and gentle skin care
Use topical agents cautiously because the defective barrier permits systemic absorption and toxicity, avoiding topical calcineurin inhibitors over large areas and monitoring levels if used
Treat cutaneous and systemic infection promptly with appropriate antimicrobials, maintaining vigilance for sepsis
Manage the atopic diathesis and pruritus with antihistamines and allergen avoidance, and screen for food allergy
Monitor growth and consider anti-inflammatory or immunomodulatory therapy such as intravenous immunoglobulin or a biologic targeting the inflammatory pathway in severe disease
Provide multidisciplinary dermatology, paediatric and dietetic care, and offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive SPINK5 inheritance
